analogy.p: Imagine a crowd of people split into two groups wearing opposite coloured shirts, standing in rigid rows in a hall (the solid lattice) – nobody can move or carry anything. Melt the lattice and the doors open: the crowd is free to wander. Now put a magnet-like 'pull' at each end of the hall: one end draws in people in red shirts, the other draws in people in blue shirts. People handing over or receiving a ticket (electrons) at the exits are like the ions being discharged. The analogy breaks down because real ions are not people who choose to move: they are pulled by the electric field, and the 'tickets' (electrons) travel round the outside wires, not through the hall.
analogy.t: A hall of people held in rows

bullets: **Electrolysis** = breaking down an ionic compound using electricity when it is molten or in solution.
The liquid that conducts the electricity and is decomposed is the **electrolyte**.
The solid rods or plates that carry the current into and out of the electrolyte are the **electrodes**.
Electrolysis is a **decomposition** reaction, and it needs a continuous supply of electrical energy to keep going.
The products are the elements that made up the compound: normally a **metal** and a **non-metal** for a molten binary ionic compound.
It is used industrially to extract reactive metals, make chlorine and sodium hydroxide, and to purify and electroplate metals (some of these are covered in separate spec points).
core.p: **Electrolysis** is the decomposition of an **ionic compound** using an **electric current**. The ionic compound must be either **molten** (melted) or **dissolved in water** so that it forms a liquid called the **electrolyte**. When a direct current is passed through the electrolyte, the compound is broken down (decomposed) into its elements. The word itself tells you this: 'lysis' means splitting, so electrolysis is splitting using electricity. It is a way of forcing a chemical change that would not happen on its own.

bullets: **Solid** ionic compound: ions locked in the lattice, so it does **not** conduct and electrolysis cannot happen.
**Molten** ionic compound: the lattice has melted, ions are **free to move**, so it conducts and is an electrolyte.
**Dissolved** ionic compound: ions are separated by water and free to move, so the solution conducts.
In **metals**, the charge carriers are **delocalised electrons**; in electrolytes the charge carriers are **ions**.
A metal conductor is not changed by the current, but an electrolyte is **decomposed**, because ions are discharged at the electrodes.
Always write 'ions are **free to move**' (not just 'the ions move') in a mark scheme answer about conduction.
Covalent compounds (e.g. sugar, ethanol) have no ions, so they do not conduct and cannot be electrolysed.
core.h: Why the ions must be free to move
core.p: A solid ionic compound is a giant **ionic lattice**: oppositely charged ions held in fixed positions by very strong **electrostatic forces of attraction**. Because the ions cannot move, a solid ionic compound **cannot conduct electricity**, and there are no delocalised electrons to carry charge either. When the compound is **melted**, the lattice breaks down and the ions become **free to move** through the liquid. The same happens when the compound **dissolves in water**, because the water separates the ions. Free-moving charged ions can now carry the current through the liquid, which is the key idea examiners look for.

bullets: **Anode** = positive electrode (connected to the + terminal of the supply).
**Cathode** = negative electrode (connected to the − terminal).
Memory aid **PANIC**: **P**ositive **A**node, **N**egative **I**s **C**athode.
**Inert electrodes** (graphite or platinum) do not take part in the reaction, so the products come only from the electrolyte.
A **direct current (d.c.)** is needed so that the electrodes keep the same charge; alternating current would keep swapping the electrodes.
Electrons travel through the **wires** in the external circuit; ions travel through the **electrolyte**.
Molten electrolytes must be heated strongly, so molten electrolysis in school is done in a **fume cupboard**.
core.p: An electrolysis cell has four main parts: a **d.c. power supply** (such as a battery), two **electrodes**, the **electrolyte**, and a container such as a beaker or crucible. The electrodes are connected to the power supply by wires, and the circuit is completed by the ions moving through the electrolyte. The electrode connected to the **positive** terminal of the supply is the **anode**, and the electrode connected to the **negative** terminal is the **cathode**. Electrodes are often made of **graphite (carbon)** or platinum because these are **inert**: they do not react with the electrolyte or the products.

bullets: **Positive ions** (metal ions, and hydrogen ions in solution) move to the **cathode**.
**Negative ions** (non-metal ions, and hydroxide ions in solution) move to the **anode**.
The ions move because of the **electric field** set up between the oppositely charged electrodes.
On reaching an electrode an ion is **discharged**: the charge on it is removed by electron transfer.
Electrons are **pushed into** the cathode by the supply, and **pulled out of** the anode by the supply.
The cathode has an excess of electrons, which is why it attracts positive ions.
Because the compound is being used up, the electrolyte is **decomposed** and the reaction cannot be reversed by the same cell.
core.p: Opposite charges attract. During electrolysis, **positive ions (cations)** are attracted to the **negative electrode (cathode)**, and **negative ions (anions)** are attracted to the **positive electrode (anode)**. This movement of ions is the current flowing inside the electrolyte. When an ion reaches an electrode it is **discharged**, which means it gains or loses electrons to become an uncharged atom. The ions then leave the electrolyte as products, so the electrolyte is gradually used up.

bullets: Cathode reaction = **reduction** (positive ions **gain** electrons to form atoms).
Anode reaction = **oxidation** (negative ions **lose** electrons to form atoms or molecules).
Electrons lost at the anode = electrons gained at the cathode, so the electrons are **conserved**.
The electrons flow from the anode, through the wire and power supply, to the cathode.
Overall the cell turns **electrical energy into chemical energy**: it forces a non-spontaneous decomposition.
**Higher tier**: you must be able to write and balance **half equations** for these electrode reactions.
Metals are formed at the cathode because metal ions are positive and are **reduced**.
core.h: Reduction at the cathode and oxidation at the anode
core.p: At the **cathode**, positive ions **gain electrons**. Gain of electrons is **reduction**. At the **anode**, negative ions **lose electrons**. Loss of electrons is **oxidation**. Remember **OIL RIG**: **O**xidation **I**s **L**oss, **R**eduction **I**s **G**ain (of electrons). The electrons lost at the anode travel round the external circuit through the power supply and are pushed back onto the cathode, so the number of electrons gained at one electrode equals the number lost at the other. This is why both reactions happen together and why electrons never enter the electrolyte.

bullets: Cathode (reduction): electrons on the **left**: e.g. Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na, Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb, Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al.
Anode (oxidation): electrons on the **right**: e.g. 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻, 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻, 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻.
Check **charge**: total charge on the left must equal total charge on the right (e.g. +2 + (−2) = 0 for Pb).
Check **atoms**: halogens and oxygen leave as molecules (Cl₂, Br₂, I₂, O₂), so write 2 ions and a diatomic product.
Use the **state symbols** only if asked; otherwise a balanced equation with electrons is what earns the mark.
Number of electrons = the size of the ion's charge (for each ion discharged).
To combine two half equations into an overall equation, multiply so the number of electrons is **equal**, then add and cancel the electrons.
core.p: A **half equation** shows only one electrode reaction, with electrons written explicitly. At the cathode the electrons appear on the **left** (reactants), because they are gained. At the anode the electrons appear on the **right** (products), because they are lost. A half equation must balance in **atoms** and also in **charge**. For example, a lead(II) ion has a 2+ charge, so it needs 2 electrons to become a neutral atom: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb. Non-metal elements such as bromine and chlorine are diatomic, so two ions must be discharged to make one molecule: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.

bullets: Ions present in the melt: **Pb²⁺** and **Br⁻** only.
**Cathode (−)**: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb. A **silver-grey bead of molten lead** forms and sinks to the bottom (lead is dense).
**Anode (+)**: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻. **Brown (orange-brown) bromine gas** is given off.
Overall: PbBr₂(l) → Pb(l) + Br₂(g).
The experiment is done in a **fume cupboard** because bromine vapour is toxic and corrosive, and lead compounds are toxic.
Wear eye protection; take care with hot equipment as the crucible and melt are at several hundred degrees.
The solid does not conduct, so the bulb or ammeter only reads when the lead bromide is **molten**.
core.h: Electrolysis of molten lead bromide: step by step
core.p: Molten **lead(II) bromide** (PbBr₂) is the classic example because it has only two types of ion, so there is no choice about what forms at each electrode. The solid is heated in a crucible above its melting point (about 370 °C) in a **fume cupboard** until it melts. Two inert **graphite electrodes** are placed in the molten liquid and connected to a d.c. supply. Lead ions are attracted to the cathode and bromide ions to the anode, so the compound is decomposed into its elements.

bullets: Molten NaCl: cathode Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na; anode 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; overall 2NaCl → 2Na + Cl₂.
Molten ZnCl₂: cathode Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn; anode 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; overall ZnCl₂ → Zn + Cl₂.
Molten MgO: cathode Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg; anode 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻; overall 2MgO → 2Mg + O₂.
Molten KI: cathode K⁺ + e⁻ → K; anode 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻ (purple iodine vapour).
**Chlorine** gas is a pale green, toxic gas that **bleaches damp litmus paper**.
Oxygen at a **graphite anode** can react with the hot carbon to form carbon dioxide, so graphite anodes may be burnt away and need replacing (important in aluminium extraction).
Always include the **state** of the electrolyte (l) to make clear it is molten, not aqueous.
core.p: The same pattern works for any simple molten ionic compound containing a metal ion and a non-metal ion. The metal ion always goes to the cathode and forms the metal; the non-metal ion goes to the anode and forms the non-metal. Molten **sodium chloride** gives sodium and chlorine; molten **zinc chloride** gives zinc and chlorine; molten **magnesium oxide** gives magnesium and oxygen. This pattern is only straightforward in **molten** liquids, where there is no water to add extra ions (compare the electrolysis of aqueous solutions).

bullets: Step 1: write the formula and name the **ions** (e.g. MgCl₂ → Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻).
Step 2: **cathode** = the metal (e.g. magnesium).
Step 3: **anode** = the non-metal (e.g. chlorine, written Cl₂).
Diatomic products: **H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂** are written as molecules.
If the compound has the ratio 1:2 (MgCl₂), 2Cl⁻ ions give one Cl₂ molecule, matching the formula.
A good check: the ratio of products in the overall equation should match the formula of the compound.
Examiners often give the formula of an unfamiliar ionic compound, so learn the rule rather than specific examples.
core.h: Predicting the products of molten electrolysis
core.p: For a molten binary ionic compound you can predict the products in three quick steps. First, identify the two ions in the compound. Second, the **positive ion goes to the cathode** and is reduced to the **metal**. Third, the **negative ion goes to the anode** and is oxidised to the **non-metal**. There is no alternative ion to compete, because the melt contains only the two ions from the compound. This is why molten electrolysis is easier to predict than electrolysis of aqueous solutions.

bullets: Carbon can only displace (reduce) metals **below it** in the reactivity series.
Aluminium is **more reactive than carbon**, so aluminium oxide must be electrolysed (see the point on extraction of aluminium).
A very reactive metal holds on to its oxygen tightly, so a strong reducing method (electrolysis) is needed.
Electrolysis supplies **electrons** directly to the metal ions: **reduction** without carbon.
The compound has to be **molten** so the metal ions are free to move to the cathode.
Metals very low in the series (gold, silver) may be found **uncombined (native)** and need no chemical extraction.
The method chosen depends on reactivity, cost, and energy required.
core.p: The **reactivity series** decides how a metal is extracted from its ore. Metals **less reactive than carbon** (such as iron and zinc) can be extracted by **reduction with carbon**, because carbon is more reactive and takes the oxygen from the metal oxide. Metals **more reactive than carbon** (such as aluminium, calcium, magnesium, sodium and potassium) cannot be reduced by carbon, so they are extracted by **electrolysis of their molten compounds**. The metal ions are reduced at the cathode by gaining electrons supplied by the electric current.

bullets: High melting points of ionic compounds mean a large **heating cost** to keep the electrolyte molten.
The **electricity** needed to decompose the compound is a second large cost.
This is why reactive metals such as aluminium are historically more expensive than iron.
Carbon is cheaper and works at lower temperatures, so it is preferred whenever the metal is below carbon in reactivity.
Companies reduce costs by lowering melting points (e.g. adding another substance so the electrolyte melts at a lower temperature) and by recycling the metal.
Recycling metals uses much less energy than extracting them again from ores.
core.h: Cost and energy: why electrolysis is expensive
core.p: Electrolysis is a more **expensive** process than reduction with carbon. A large amount of **energy** is needed to melt the ionic compound, because the strong electrostatic forces in the giant ionic lattice give it a very high melting point. A further large amount of **electrical energy** is needed to drive the electrolysis itself. In industry, the cost of heating and electricity is a major cost, so electrolysis plants are often located near cheap electricity (for example hydroelectric power).

bullets: Lead: **silver-grey** molten bead at the cathode; bromine: **brown** vapour at the anode.
Chlorine: **bleaches damp (blue) litmus paper**, pale green gas, toxic.
Oxygen: **relights a glowing splint**.
Hydrogen: **squeaky pop** with a lit splint (more relevant to aqueous electrolysis).
An ammeter or lamp showing a **current** confirms that the electrolyte is conducting.
Bubbles at an electrode indicate gas being formed.
Risks: toxic gases (chlorine, bromine) mean the work must be in a **fume cupboard**; hot molten salts need careful handling.
core.p: In a lab electrolysis you are expected to link observations to the products. The cathode shows the metal forming, and the anode shows a gas forming (or sometimes a liquid or solid for iodine). A d.c. supply connected to a lamp or ammeter shows that current flows only when the substance is molten or dissolved. Gas tests are used to identify what is made: chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper, oxygen relights a glowing splint, hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint.

bullets: Link to **bonding**: strong electrostatic forces → high melting points → expensive to melt.
Link to **reactivity series**: decides whether carbon or electrolysis is needed.
Link to **redox**: reduction at cathode, oxidation at anode (OIL RIG).
Link to **aluminium extraction**: aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten **cryolite** to lower the melting point and save energy.
Link to **aqueous electrolysis**: with water present, H⁺ and OH⁻ ions also compete, so products can differ from the molten case.
Link to **calculations**: moles of electrons = charge on the ion × moles of ion discharged.
Higher tier: be ready to deduce half equations for unfamiliar ions from their charge.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: Electrolysis brings together several parts of the course. It relies on **ionic bonding and structure** (why the ions are fixed in a solid and free in a liquid), on the **reactivity series** (which metals need electrolysis), on **oxidation and reduction** (electron transfer), and on **energy** (the cost of heating and electricity). At Higher tier, you also need to write **half equations** and balance them, and later you will see this idea applied to the extraction of **aluminium** (with cryolite) and to the electrolysis of **aqueous solutions**, where water adds extra ions that compete at the electrodes.

exam: Command words: **State** (1 mark, short fact), **Describe** (what happens, in order), **Explain** (give the reason: use 'because'), **Write a half equation** (balance atoms and charge).
For 'why does a solid ionic compound not conduct?' write: ions are in **fixed positions** (in a lattice) and **cannot move**/are not free to move.
For 'why does a molten ionic compound conduct?' write: the **ions are free to move** and carry the charge.
Always say which ion goes to which electrode and why: **positive ions attracted to the cathode (negative electrode)**.
For 2 mark half equation questions: 1 mark for correct formulae, 1 mark for correct balancing (electrons on the correct side).
For molten electrolysis, name the **product** at each electrode: metal at cathode, non-metal at anode.
To explain why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis (3 marks): aluminium is **more reactive than carbon**; so **carbon cannot reduce** aluminium oxide; so electrolysis is used.
4 mark questions on the electrolysis of molten lead bromide: ions, movement to electrodes, products with observations, and the safety precaution (fume cupboard).
Explain **why electrolysis is expensive**: needs a lot of energy to **melt** the compound and a lot of **electricity**.
Write ion charges correctly (e.g. Pb²⁺, Br⁻) and give **state symbols** (l), (g) when asked; molten means (l), not (aq).
For 6 mark questions: structure your answer logically (apparatus, ions, movement, electrode reactions with half equations, products, observations, safety, cost).

mistakes.r: Ions carry the current through the electrolyte; electrons flow through the wires in the external circuit.
The ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice by strong electrostatic forces, so they are not free to move.
mistakes.w: Solid sodium chloride doesn't conduct because it has no electrons or the ions are not charged.

mistakes.r: The anode is the positive electrode and the cathode is the negative electrode (PANIC).
The compound is melted by heat, and decomposed by the electric current.
mistakes.w: The compound is decomposed by heat.

mistakes.r: Chlorine and bromine are diatomic molecules: write Cl₂ and Br₂.
mistakes.w: Writing the product as Cl or Br (single atoms).

mistakes.r: At the anode electrons are lost, so they appear on the right: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.
mistakes.w: Writing 2Br⁻ + 2e⁻ → Br₂ (electrons on the wrong side).

mistakes.r: Metal ions are positive, are attracted to the cathode and are reduced there.
mistakes.w: A metal is formed at the anode.

mistakes.r: Electrolysis is expensive because of the energy to melt the compound and the electricity needed; it is used only for metals more reactive than carbon.
mistakes.w: Electrolysis is a cheap way to extract all metals.

summary: You must know that electrolysis uses an electric current to decompose a molten or dissolved ionic compound because its ions are free to move, that positive ions move to the cathode and negative ions to the anode, and that the products at each electrode can be predicted (and, at Higher tier, written as half equations). It matters because it is how reactive metals above carbon in the reactivity series are extracted.

terms.d: The decomposition of an ionic compound using an electric current when it is molten or dissolved in water.
The molten or dissolved ionic compound that conducts electricity and is decomposed during electrolysis.
A solid conductor (often graphite or platinum) that carries electric current into or out of the electrolyte.
An electrode that does not react with the electrolyte or the products of electrolysis, e.g. graphite or platinum.
The positive electrode, to which negative ions are attracted and where oxidation occurs.
The negative electrode, to which positive ions are attracted and where reduction occurs.
A positively charged ion; moves to the cathode during electrolysis.
A negatively charged ion; moves to the anode during electrolysis.
A giant regular arrangement of oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
Melted; in a molten ionic compound the lattice has broken down and the ions are free to move.
A reaction in which a compound is broken down into simpler substances (elements or smaller compounds).
Gain of electrons; occurs at the cathode (OIL RIG).
Loss of electrons; occurs at the anode (OIL RIG).
An equation showing the reaction at one electrode, with electrons included and balanced for atoms and charge.
An ion is discharged when it gains or loses electrons at an electrode to become an uncharged atom or molecule.
A list of metals in order of reactivity, used to decide how a metal is extracted from its ore.
A rock that contains enough of a metal compound for the metal to be extracted economically.
Current that flows in one direction only, keeping the electrodes the same charge.

worked.ans: Cathode: zinc, Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn. Anode: chlorine gas, 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. Overall: ZnCl₂(l) → Zn(l) + Cl₂(g).
worked.q: Molten zinc chloride, ZnCl₂, is electrolysed using inert electrodes. State the products at the cathode and anode and write a half equation for each electrode. (4 marks)
steps: Ions present: Zn²⁺ and Cl⁻ only (no water, so no other ions).
Zn²⁺ is positive so goes to the cathode, where it gains 2 electrons (reduction): Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn.
Cl⁻ is negative so goes to the anode, where it loses electrons (oxidation); chlorine is diatomic: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.

worked.ans: In solid NaCl the ions are in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move, so it cannot conduct. When molten, the ions are free to move and carry charge, so it conducts.
worked.q: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten sodium chloride does. (3 marks)
steps: Solid: sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice; the ions are held in fixed positions by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
The ions cannot move, so there are no charge carriers.
Molten: the lattice breaks down, so the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are free to move and carry the current.

worked.ans: Cathode: Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg. Anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻. Overall: 2MgO(l) → 2Mg(l) + O₂(g).
worked.q: Molten magnesium oxide is electrolysed. Write the half equations and the overall equation. (Higher tier, 4 marks)
steps: Electrons must be equal: multiply the cathode equation by 2: 2Mg²⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2Mg.
Add the equations and cancel 4e⁻: 2Mg²⁺ + 2O²⁻ → 2Mg + O₂, i.e. 2MgO → 2Mg + O₂.
